similar: Bruce Springsteen & The E Street Band
info.bio:
Bruce Frederick Joseph Springsteen Zirilli. Nació en Freehold, New Jersey, EE UU, el 23 de septiembre de 1949 de padre irlandés (Douglas Springsteen) y de madre italiana (Adele Zirilli). Creció en Freehold, Nueva Jersey.

Editó su primer disco en 1972, llamado "Greetings from Asbury Park", que vendió apenas 25.000 copias y tuvo poca acogida por la crítica. Su siguiente disco fue "The Wild, the Innocent and the E street Shuffle", editado al año siguiente, que tuvo una repercusión mayor.

scenes.name: Reacción rockista y new americana
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Contra las «bandas inglesas con peinados raros», el regreso de la autenticidad: Rolling Stone denuncia que MTV vendió el rock'n'roll, Greil Marcus y Dave Marsh acusan al new pop de vacuidad e imperialismo británico. Antiguos punks se disfrazan de sureños alcohólicos (The Blasters, Violent Femmes, The Gun Club, Lone Justice, Blood on the Saddle) y triunfan Springsteen, Mellencamp y Fogerty. Pero Prince, «Beat It», ZZ Top, Van Halen o los remixes de Arthur Baker para Born in the U.S.A. aprenden del new pop; a la larga el hip hop heredará las fantasías de rebelión callejera.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

scenes.name: Roots-rock de los ochenta y cow-punk
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Como en 1970 tras 1966, la new wave de 1976 va seguida de un revival del roots-rock, esta vez gradual y disfrazado: punks que desfiguran los estilos tradicionales (X, Dream Syndicate, Gun Club) y los «cow-punks» que tocan country ambientado entre inadaptados: Long Ryders, Jason & The Scorchers, Fetchin Bones, Lone Justice, Beat Farmers. El populismo de Los Lobos, Del Fuegos, Del-Lords y Walkabouts; en la Costa Oeste, los dementes Camper Van Beethoven, Donner Party, Catheads, Thin White Rope y los American Music Club de Mark Eitzel; en Texas, Wild Seeds, Poi Dog Pondering, Glass Eye; en los Grandes Lagos, BoDeans, Soul Asylum, Afghan Whigs, Shrimp Boat y los canadienses Cowboy Junkies. Nashville se renueva con los neotradicionalistas (George Strait, Randy Travis, Garth Brooks, Lyle Lovett, Steve Earle, Dwight Yoakam) y el surf instrumental vuelve con Shadowy Men On A Shadowy Planet.

podcast.title: Experiment with Numbered Wristbands (Pre-1974)
podcast.body: Bill Graham implemented an experimental ticketing policy involving numbered wristbands, which was first tried with a Bruce Springsteen show. Attendees would receive a wristband at the box office, and a random number would be drawn to determine the first person in line, with others following in sequential order. "The first experiment was with a Bruce Springsteen show, and it worked like this."

podcast.title: 2023 Tour Dynamic Pricing Controversy
podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen's 2023 tour generated significant controversy due to its use of dynamic pricing, with initial reports of "horror stories" in the news about nosebleed seats being listed for up to $5,000. However, demand eventually softened, causing prices to fall, with some secondary sellers offering tickets with a $59 face value for as low as $5 for certain shows. "For example, when Bruce Springsteen started selling tickets for his 2023 tour, horror stories appeared in the news involving dynamic pricing."

podcast.title: Majority of 2023 Tour Tickets Under $100
podcast.body: Despite the initial controversy surrounding dynamic pricing for his 2023 tour, the majority of Bruce Springsteen's tickets ultimately sold for less than $100. This demonstrated that while extreme prices grabbed headlines, affordable options were still prevalent for many concertgoers. "When all was said and done, the majority of tickets for that Springsteen tour sold for less than $100."

podcast.title: "Deuce Coupes" Reference
podcast.body: The lyric "revved up like a deuce" in "Blinded by the Light" refers to a hot rod engine, specifically one associated with three models of Ford cars from the 1930s known as "deuce coupes." These cars were once favorites of hot rod modifiers. "Springsteen is singing about revving up a four cylinder engine and not anything else, including any feminine hygiene products."

podcast.title: 21st Century Legacy Artist
podcast.body: Springsteen is identified as a "legacy artist" who, alongside U2 and Radiohead, continues to actively push for social and political change through music in the 21st century, contrasting with the more introspective approach of many contemporary artists. "it's legacy artists, radio heads, Springsteen, U2, that continue to push for change through music while newer artists generally stay away from this area."

podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen has an asteroid named in his honor, a piece of space rock bearing his name. "Eric Clapton, Brian Wilson, ZZ Topp, Yes, Bruce Springsteen, and Jimmy Page are among those with their own pieces of space rock."

podcast.title: Audience Expectations in Rock
podcast.body: Springsteen reflected on rock music as a "house of dreams" where artists serve the audience's imagination. He noted that once an artist has left "fingerprints" there, crossing that imagination can have "grave consequences," highlighting the personal and challenging nature of evolving artistically. "It's a house of dreams, of illusions, of role playing and artist audience transference. You serve at the behest of your audience's imagination. That's a very personal place."

podcast.title: Briefly Labeled "Punk" (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, the term "punk rock" was thrown around carelessly, and even Bruce Springsteen was, at one point, called a "punk." "By the middle of the 70s, the term was being thrown around very carelessly, very liberally. Patty Smith was called a punk. And then so was Eros Smith and Bruce Springsteen, even the Rolling Stones."

podcast.title: Catalog Sale (2020s)
podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen sold his music catalog for $550 million, participating in a major trend where artists monetized their life's work for upfront financial security and tax advantages. This "gold rush" for catalogs saw companies like Primary Wave and Hypnosis Song Fund acquiring music rights, benefiting artists with immediate cash and ensuring their music's long-term public consciousness. "Bruce Springsteen got 550 million."

podcast.title: Early Career Recognition
podcast.body: In January 1973, Robert Hillburn, a music critic for the Los Angeles Times, included Bruce Springsteen as one of three "unknowns" in a lengthy article titled "Good Luck to Three Friends Who Will Need It." Hillburn noted Springsteen's potential, stating, "Springsteen has potential, and I'll play his next album the day I get it. If things break right, I may even play this one some more." "Springsteen was one of those unknowns."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Extensive Encore Performances
podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen was known for his long and committed encore performances. Even after playing sets that lasted three or four hours, he would routinely return to the stage to perform additional songs, often multiple times. "Even after playing for three or four hours, he'd stagger back on stage to play one more song, time and time again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Imperial Status Boosts Imitators
podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen's imperial "blowup" in the mid-80s, marked by seven top ten hits from "Born in the USA," led radio stations to revive "On the Dark Side," a 1983 single from the flop movie soundtrack *Eddie and the Cruisers* by John Cafferty and the Beaver Brown Band. This song, which sounded "an awful lot like Springsteen and the East Street band," belatedly became a top ten hit in the fall of 1984, proving that even his imitators could score on the charts due to his pop star status. "That's how you know that Bruce was finally a pop star even his imitators were scoring on the charts."

podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen invited The Trews to perform "Twist and Shout" with him during an encore. The unexpected collaboration resulted in a 12-minute performance that is available on YouTube. "if you look up Bruce Springsteen with the trues, it's there's that version's on YouTube."

podcast.title: Interaction with The Trews
podcast.body: Despite his reputation for not socializing before shows, Bruce Springsteen drove his golf cart directly up to The Trews and engaged them in a brief, energetic conversation, asking where they were from. This direct interaction left a strong impression on the band. "He just came right up and he's like, how you doing? We're like, oh, good man. Good, Bruce Springsteen. We're good."

podcast.title: Jokes About We Are The World Recording
podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen was present at the recording of "We Are The World" and continued to joke about the experience 15 years later. His anecdotes included humorous comments about things that occurred during the session, such as "being asked questions about makeup in the recording studio, including all the women." "15 años después, Bruce Springson se seguía creciendo... era una amigotada graciosa."

podcast.title: Legal Issues with Michael Pell
podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen experienced a period of "musical limbo" stemming from a legal dispute with his former manager, Michael Pell. This situation affected his creative output, including the initial development of the music and chorus for "Because the Night." "Bruce wrote the music and the chorus, but he was kind of in a musical limbo because of the legal drama with his former manager, Michael Pell."

"He got inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and recorded a live TV special, a black and white night, where he was joined by Elvis's 70s backing band, Bruce Springsteen, Elvis Costello, K.D. podcast.title: Opposition to Trump Campaign Music Use
podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen was among a long list of artists who expressed strong opposition to Donald Trump's campaign using their music at political rallies. Despite venues often holding blanket performing rights licenses, artists did not want their work associated with the campaign and many pursued cease and desist orders or lawsuits. podcast.title: Reagan's Misappropriation
podcast.body: In 1984, Ronald Reagan, while running for reelection, publicly praised Bruce Springsteen, stating that "America's future rest in a thousand dreams inside your hearts. It rests in the message of hope in songs of a man so many young Americans admire New Jersey's own Bruce Springsteen." Reagan, however, was later criticized for missing the critical, anti-war message embedded in the verses of "Born in the U.S.A.," focusing only on the celebratory chorus. "America's future rest in a thousand dreams inside your hearts. It rests in the message of hope in songs of a man so many young Americans admire New Jersey's own Bruce Springsteen."

podcast.title: Signature Characteristics
podcast.body: Bruce Springsteen is renowned for his portrayal as a voice for the everyman, for creating songs populated with recognizable characters, and for expressing familiar working-class attitudes, dreams, and problems. He often acknowledges historical figures, maintains a politically aware and socially conscious stance, and backs these up with significant activism. His work typically includes anthemic songs that predominantly convey messages of hope through poetic lyrics and highly energetic live performances. "A voice for the everyman, recognizable characters in his songs. Familiar working class attitudes, dreams, and problems. Acknowledgement of historical figures. Politically aware, socially conscious, plenty of activism to back it up. Anthemic songs, messages of hope, mostly anyway, poetic lyrics, and highly energetic live performances."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Songwriting Philosophy
podcast.body: Springsteen, a native of Freehold, New Jersey, articulated his songwriting approach to NPR's Terry Gross, explaining that the hope in his songs is typically found in the chorus, while the detailed, often darker, stories are conveyed within the verses. This distinction is crucial for understanding the depth and often misunderstood messages in his work, such as "Born in the U.S.A." "springstein who as most people know is from freehold New Jersey told NPR is Terry gross that the hope. In his songs can be found in the chorus and the details of the story are in the verses."

podcast.title: Unexpected Entrance
podcast.body: Prior to his performance in Moncton, Bruce Springsteen's road manager indicated he rarely met with opening acts due to his long pre-show preparations. However, Springsteen made a dramatic and unexpected entrance, driving a golf cart onto the grounds with Little Steven and drummer Max Weinberg, displaying incredible energy that made him seem "14 years old." podcast.title: Veteran's Appreciation of "Born in the U.S.A."
podcast.body: The first person outside the E Street Band to hear the finished version of "Born in the U.S.A." was Bobby Mueller, president of the Vietnam Veterans of America, who reportedly smiled, appreciating the song's message. He understood that the song was not praising America, but rather highlighting the betrayal faced by those who served their country, particularly veterans who returned home unable to find jobs. "the first person outside of the East Street band to hear the finished version of born in the USA was Bobby Mueller the president of the Vietnam veterans of America who smiled presumably because he appreciated the songs message about not the best part of America but the betrayal of America a betrayal of people who died in service for their country and came home and could not find a job."

xref.title: Acquisition of ATV Music (1985)
xref.body: In 1985, Michael Jackson outbid Paul McCartney to purchase the ATV Music catalog for $47.5 million. This catalog included 4,000 songs, notably 250 by The Beatles (almost their entire output), as well as tracks by The Rolling Stones, Elvis, and Bruce Springsteen. "In 1985, ATV Music, that company with the Beatles publishing, went up for sale. Four thousand songs, including 250 from the Beatles, which is pretty much everything they ever wrote, as well as tracks by the Rolling Stones, Elvis and Bruce Springsteen. Jackson then outbid McCartney, paying $47.5 million for this catalog."

In 1985, ATV Music, that company with the Beatles publishing, went up for sale. xref.title: Catalog Sale to Hypnosis Song Fund (Early 2023)
xref.body: Justin Bieber sold his music catalog to the Hypnosis Song Fund for $200 million in early 2023. This was noted as Merck Mercuriatis's biggest acquisition to that point. His catalog's value is also bolstered by his large streaming audience, with 80 million monthly listeners on Spotify compared to Bruce Springsteen's 17 million. "Justin Bieber $200 million." "Merck's biggest acquisition to this point has been Justin Bieber's catalog. This happened in early 2023, for which Bieber was paid $200 million." "Justin Bieber's fans have 60 years or 70 years in front of them as opposed to 30 years in front of them. That makes sense.
